blocks.text: Kindle it with much smoke. Τῦφε δὲ καίων δίωκε· ὁ γαρ καπνὸς διώκει τὰς μελισσας, καὶ τὰς σφῆκας [Typhe de kaiōn diōke; ho gar kapnos diōkei tas melissas, kai tas sphēkas]. The word τῦφε [typhe] means: Burning, pursue: for smoke pursues bees and wasps. Columella, book 9, chapter 15, §5, where he speaks of taking the honey from beehives: When the hive has been opened at the back, where there is no entrance, we shall apply smoke made from galbanum, or from dry smoke (perhaps hay) ^{(5)}. And below: The smoke is driven toward the bees, which at once, unable to bear the reek, betake themselves to the front part of their dwelling, and sometimes outside the entrance. Pliny, book 11, ch. 16: When the honey is taken out, it is most useful to drive the bees off with smoke, so that they do not become angry or greedily devour it themselves. With more frequent smoke their sluggishness is also roused to work. In Greek this is called βλίσαι [blisai] and ἐναύειν [enauein]. Hesychius: Βλίσαι· [III, 362] καπνίσαι μελίσσας, καὶ ἐξελάσαι τῶν σκηνῶν [Blisai; kapnisai melissas, kai exelasai tōn skēnōn] (read σμηνῶν [smēnōn]). To fumigate bees and drive them out of their hives. Likewise, ἐναύοντες· ἀνάπτοντες πυρί. τὰ γὰρ σμήνη τῶν μελισσῶν διώκουσι διὰ πυρὸς καὶ καπνοῦ [enauontes; anaptontes pyri. ta gar smēnē tōn melissōn diōkousi dia pyros kai kapnou]: Kindling fire: for they pursue swarms of bees with fire and smoke. And in Arabic جلا [jalā] giala. Alcamus: جلا النحل دخن عليها ليشتار العسل [jalā al-naḥl dakhkhana ʿalayhā li-yashtār al-ʿasal] Giala the bee, that is, he fumigated it, in order to take the honey out of the hive. In the Talmud, tractate Kelim, ch. 16, §7, p. 26a, the Glossator explains what מדף של דבורים, the maddaph of bees, is, as follows: כלי שמשימין בו אש וגללי בקר ומעשנים שיברחו מן הכוורת הנחילים ויקח הדבש מלשון אשר תדפנו רוח, It is a vessel in which fire and cow dung are placed, by whose fumigation the bees are put to flight from the hive, so that the honey may be taken (it is derived from the verb נדף, to drive away): whence Psal. I, 4: “The wind drives it away.” From this fumigation, moreover, the poets everywhere draw similes, as Moses does in this passage, if we follow the Syriac, Chaldee and Arabic versions. Lycophron on Paris, line 180:

Χ' ὡμὲν παλιμπόρευτον ἵξεται τρίβον, Σφῆκας δαφοινὲς χηράμων ἀνειρύσας, Ὁποῖα κοῦρος δῶμα κινήσας καπνῷ· [Ch' hōmen palimporeuton hixetai tribon, Sphēkas daphoines chēramōn aneirysas, Hopoia kouros dōma kinēsas kapnōi;]
And he indeed will go back by the way he came, drawing blood-red wasps out of their holes, as when a boy has smoked out a hive.
That is, having carried off Helen and returning to Troy, he will provoke the Greeks, as wasps and bees are provoked by smoke. And at line 254 the same poet says of the Greeks:
Ἀλλ' ὡς μέλισσαι συμπεφυρμέναι καπνῷ. [All' hōs melissai sympephyrmenai kapnōi.]
But like bees mingled with smoke, etc. See the rest there. Apollonius, Argonautica book 2, line 29:

Λευγαλέως Βέβρυκας ὑπερφιάλους ἐφόβησαν· Ὡς δὲ μελισσάων σμῆνος μέγα μηλοβοτῆρες, Ἠὲ μελισσοκόμοι, πέτρῃ ἔνι καπνιόωσιν· Αἱ δή τοι τείως μὲν ἀολλέες ᾧ ἐνὶ σίμβλῳ Βομβηδὸν κλονέονται, ἐπιπρὸ δὲ λιγνυόεντι Καπνῷ τυφόμεναι πέτρης ἑκὰς ἀΐσσουσιν. [Leugaleōs Bebrykas hyperphialous ephobēsan; Hōs de melissaōn smēnos mega mēlobotēres, Ēe melissokomoi, petrēi eni kapnioōsin; Hai dē toi teiōs men aollees hōi eni simblōi Bombēdon kloneontai, epipro de lignyoenti Kapnōi typhomenai petrēs hekas aïssousin.]

They sorely terrified the arrogant Bebryces, as shepherds or beekeepers fumigate a great swarm of bees in a rock. These meanwhile, crowded together in their hive [col. 509] , are thrown into confusion with a buzzing, but, scorched beyond measure by the sooty smoke, they pour out far from the rock. Here the Scholiast writes that bees flee smoke διὰ τὸ στενόπωρον [III, 363] εἶναι αὐτῶν τὴν ὄσφρησιν [dia to stenopōron einai autōn tēn osphrēsin], because their organs of smell have very narrow passages. Virgil, of the people of Lavinium besieged in their city by Aeneas, Aeneid book 12:

Others bear arms and press on to defend the walls: as when a shepherd has tracked bees shut up in a hollow rock and filled it with bitter smoke. They within, alarmed for their safety, run to and fro through their waxen camp and whet their anger with loud buzzing. The black reek rolls through the dwelling; now the rocks within resound with a hidden murmur, and the smoke goes up into the empty air.
Quintus Smyrnaeus, on Ajax defending the carcass of Achilles against the Trojans, book 3, line 217:

— — τοὶ δ᾽ οὐκ ἀπέληγον ὁμοκλῆς, Ἀλλὰ οἱ ἀμφεμάχοντο, περισταδὸν ἀΐσσοντες, Αἰὲν ἐπασσύτεροι, τανυχειλέες εὖτε μέλισσαι, Αἵθ᾽ ἑὸν περὶ σίμβλον ἀπειρέσιαι ποτέωνται, ῎Ανδρ᾽ ἀπαμυνόμεναι, ὃδ᾽ ἄρ᾽ ἐκ ἀλέγων ἐπιούσας, Κηροὺς ἐκτάμνησι μελίχροας· αἳ δ᾽ ἀκάχωνται Καπνοῦ ὑπαὶ ῥιπῆς ἠ δ᾽ ἀνέρος· ἀλλ᾽ ἄρα καὶ ὡς Ἀντίαι ἀΐσσουσιν, ὃ δ᾽ οὐκ ὄθετ᾽, οὐδ᾽ ἄρα βαιόν. [— — toi d' ouk apelēgon homoklēs, Alla hoi amphemachonto, peristadon aïssontes, Aien epassyteroi, tanycheilees eute melissai, Haith' heon peri simblon apeiresiai poteōntai, Andr' apamynomenai, hod' ar' ek alegōn epiousas, Kērous ektamnēsi melichroas; hai d' akachōntai Kapnou hypai rhipēs ē d' aneros; all' ara kai hōs Antiai aïssousin, ho d' ouk othet', oud' ara baion.]

They did not cease their threats, but attacked him, rushing in from all sides ever more thickly, like long-lipped bees that fly in countless swarms around their hive to ward off a man (gathering the honey). He, however, paying no heed to their onset, cuts out the honeyed combs. And they, although tormented by the onslaught of the smoke and of the man, still press against him. But he takes not the least account of them. Gregory of Nazianzus, in the Poem On his own life:
᾽Ανίστατ᾽ εὐθὺς ὥσπερ ἐκ καπνοῦ βίας ᾽Εσμὸς μελισσῶν· — — — [Anistat' euthys hōsper ek kapnou bias Hesmos melissōn; — — —]
At once (the people) rises up like a swarm of bees under the force of smoke.
